content:
The Cabinet Member (Environment and
Streetscene), Councillor Kath Unsworth, presented the confidential
report of the Director of Customer and Digital.
 
The report sought approval for the Shared
Fleet Strategy and for the Procurement Strategy required to
establish a supplier for fleet vehicles.
 
Members noted four main areas for
consideration, which were service delivery, finances, legal and
environmental, and finally, organisational. 
 
Resolved:
(Unanimously)
 
1.            
To approve the Shared Fleet Strategy.
2.            
To agree the Procurement Strategy as set out in paragraph 27.
3.            
To approve that the award decision is delegated to the Cabinet
Member for Environment and Streetscene through the Executive Member
Decision process.
 
Reasons for
recommendations:
 
1.            
A shared Fleet Strategy sets out the principles of fleet management
and procurement. Procuring on a contract hire basis provides a
level of cost certainty and protects front line service delivery
through allowing for relief vehicles.
2.            
A strategy that sets out replacement timelines improves
transparency with members and fleet users.
3.            
Having a single provider for fleet replacement will be more
efficient than managing multiple contracts.
 
Other options
considered and rejected:
 
1.            
To continue to procure fleet on a case-by-case basis. This has been
rejected as it limits options to utilise economies of scale. The
individual process can also be overly onerous and delay replacement
of vehicles.
2.            
To purchase vehicles outright. This has been rejected as it felt
that procuring on a contract hire basis provides greater
operational control and an increased level of cost certainty. It
also reduces the reliance on multiple third-party contractors to
undertake repairs.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Shared Fleet Strategy and Procurement Strategy for fleet vehicles.

utilised as a client contingency and for fit out purposes.
 
4.   
That the Cabinet member agrees to a £112,000 contribution
from the Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) for the creation of a
new Youth zone at Bamber Bridge Leisure Centre.
 
Reasons for
decision:
 
To ensure the
essential refurbishment works required to facilitate the creation
of the new Youth Hub at Bamber Bridge Leisure Centre are fully
funded and delivered. This includes providing a suitable, modern,
and safe environment that meets the needs of young people, supports
the intended programme of activities, and enables the effective
operation of the Youth Hub within the leisure centre.
 
Other options
considered and rejected:
 
The Council could choose not to do this
project. However, this would represent a missed opportunity to
create a new Youth Hub at Bamber Bridge Leisure Centre.

content:
Application refused for the following reasons,
as set out in the officer’s report:
 

1.     
The proposed development is contrary to the adopted and emerging
spatial strategy for Central Lancashire. The proposal would
prejudice the delivery of housing, employment and mixed-use
development on allocated sites, would be in an unsustainable
location, and would have the potential to impact on the
regeneration of the city and town centres by focusing employment
and main town centre uses outside of these areas, contrary to
Policy 1 of the Central Lancashire Core Strategy and Policies SS1
and SS2 of the emerging Central Lancashire Local Plan.
 

2.     
The proposal is inappropriate development in the Green Belt,
results in harm to purposes a), b) and c) of Green Belt and harm to
its openness. No very special circumstances exist to outweigh the
harm to the Green Belt by virtue of inappropriateness and other
harm resulting from the proposal. The proposed development is
therefore contrary to paragraphs 142, 143 and 153 of the National
Planning Policy Framework and Policy G1 of the South Ribble Local
Plan.
 

3.     
The substantial extent, scale and cumulative effect of the proposal
would be so significant, that to grant planning permission would
undermine the plan-making process of the emerging Central
Lancashire Local Plan, which is at an advanced stage, by
pre-determining decisions about the scale, location and phasing of
development that are central to the Plan. To grant planning
permission would prejudice the outcome of the plan-making process,
contrary to paragraph 50 and the overarching aims of the National
Planning Policy Framework and would undermine public confidence in
plan-making.
 

4.     
By reason of its scale, layout and degree of permanence, the
proposal would result in an adverse urbanizing influence on the
landscape resulting in substantial harm to landscape character and
resources contrary to Central Lancashire Core Strategy Policy 21
and Paragraph 135 of the National Planning Policy Framework.
 

5.     
By virtue of the height, scale and density the proposed development
would fail to respect its rural setting, with consequent detriment
to the visual amenity of the area, contrary to paragraph 135 of the
NPPF, Policy 17 of the Central Lancashire Core Strategy and Policy
G17 of the South Ribble Local Plan.
 

6.     
In respect of the sequential test requirements for main town centre
uses (offices), the applicant has failed to provide sufficient
assessment of whether there are available and suitable sites in
sequentially preferable locations, contrary to Central Lancashire
Core Strategy Policies 9 and 11 and paragraphs 91 and 95 of the
National Planning Policy Framework.
 

7.     
Insufficient information has been provided to enable a full and
proper assessment of the highways impact of the proposals. In the
absence of this information, the development would prejudice
highway safety and the free flow of traffic contrary to Policy G17
of the South Ribble Local Plan and paragraph 115 of the National
Planning Policy Framework.
 

8.     
Insufficient information has been provided to assess the impacts of
the development on archaeology. Due to the absence of intrusive
evaluation works, it is not possible to determine the likely
effects on archaeology, as the nature, significance and extent of
any archaeological remains within four areas of higher
archaeological potential is unknown, contrary to Policy 16 of the
Central Lancashire Core Strategy and paragraphs 207 and 218 of the
National Planning Policy Framework.
topline: The Planning Committee has decided to refuse a proposed development due to contravention of spatial strategy, harm to Green Belt, and other planning policy violations.

content:
Application refused for the following reasons,
as set out in the officer’s report:
 

1.     
The proposed development is contrary to the adopted and emerging
spatial strategy for Central Lancashire. The proposal would
prejudice the delivery of employment and mixed-use development on
allocated sites, would be in an unstainable location, and would
have the potential to impact on the regeneration of the city and
town centres by focusing employment and main town centre uses
outside of these areas, contrary to Policy 1 of the Central
Lancashire Core Strategy and Policy SS1 of the emerging Central
Lancashire Local Plan.
 

2.     
The proposal is inappropriate development in the Green Belt,
results in harm to purposes a), b) and c) of Green Belt and harm to
its openness. No very special circumstances exist to outweigh the
harm to the Green Belt by virtue of inappropriateness and other
harm resulting from the proposal. The proposed development is
therefore contrary to paragraphs 142, 143 and 153 of the National
Planning Policy Framework and Policy G1 of the South Ribble Local
Plan.
 

3.     
The substantial extent, scale and cumulative effect of the proposal
would be so significant, that to grant planning permission would
undermine the plan-making process of the emerging Central
Lancashire Local Plan, which is at an advanced stage, by
pre-determining decisions about the scale, location and phasing of
development that are central to the Plan. To grant planning
permission would prejudice the outcome of the plan-making process,
contrary to paragraph 50 and the overarching aims of the National
Planning Policy Framework and undermine public confidence in
plan-making.
 

4.     
By reason of its scale, layout and degree of permanence, the
proposal would result in an adverse urbanizing influence on the
landscape resulting in substantial harm to landscape character and
resources contrary to Central Lancashire Core Strategy Policy 21
and Paragraph 135 of the National Planning Policy Framework.
 

5.     
By virtue of its proposed height and scale, the development would
fail to respect its rural setting, with consequent detriment to the
visual amenity of the area, contrary to paragraph 135 of the NPPF,
Policy 17 of the Central Lancashire Core Strategy and Policy G17 of
the South Ribble Local Plan.
 

6.     
In respect of the sequential test requirements for main town centre
uses, the applicant has failed to provide sufficient assessment of
whether there are available and suitable sites in sequentially
preferable locations contrary to Central Lancashire Core Strategy
Policies 11 and paragraphs 91 and 95 of the National Planning
Policy Framework.
 

7.     
Insufficient information has been provided to assess the impacts of
the development on archaeology. Due to the absence of intrusive
evaluation works, it is not possible to determine the likely
effects on archaeology, as the nature, significance and extent of
any archaeological remains is unknown, contrary to Policy 16 of the
Central Lancashire Core Strategy and paragraphs 207 and 218 of the
National Planning Policy Framework.
 

8.     
Insufficient information has been provided to enable a full and
proper assessment of the highways impact of the proposals. In the
absence of this information, the development would prejudice
highway safety and the free flow of traffic contrary to Policy G17
of the South Ribble Local Plan and paragraph 115 of the National
Planning Policy Framework.
 

9.     
Insufficient information has been provided to enable a full and
proper assessment of the site’s Agricultural Land
Classification (ALC) and consequently any potential harm arising
from its loss, contrary to Policy 31 of the Central Lancashire Core
Strategy and Policy EN16 of the Central Lancashire Local Plan.
 

10.In the absence of an
infrastructure phasing and delivery strategy for the entire
application site, and justification for the proposed non-mains foul
drainage system, insufficient information has been provided to
demonstrate that the site would be appropriately served with foul
water infrastructure and an adequate water supply to support the
employment premises proposed, contrary to Policy 29 in the Central
Lancashire Core Strategy and National Planning Practice Guidance on
Water Supply, wastewater and water quality.

To approve the disposal of surplus

(excl. VAT)
 
Reasons for
decision:
 
Offer provides best value to the Council. -
The Council received a £20,000 offer from the supplier for

money given the original cost. The Council also advertised the
equipment for sale, receiving only one offer, which was lower than

Consideration has also been given to the other

includes; depreciation in value, as unused equipment loses value
over time; servicing saving; the lease of industrial unit, as
disposal will free space that can be leased f to generate income
for the council.
 
The proceeds from the disposal are intended to
offset Civic Centre forfeiture costs of £162,000 which were

Do nothing - As noted in the preceding
rationale for recommendations, this option has been excluded from
consideration as it would not represent best value to the
council.
 
Sell the equipment back to supplier - The
submitted offer does not represent the best value for the
council.
 
Utilise equipment at different site - The
specified units are designed exclusively for the Civic Centre and
are unsuitable for other Council assets due to the size of those
buildings.

content:
Decision made:
 

To consider the information provided
in respect of the options for the introduction of a boroughwide
Article 4 direction (Houses in Multiple Occupation) as set out in
this report including Appendices.

 

To approve the making of an
immediate Article 4 Direction under the Town and Country (General
Permitted Development) (England) Order 2015 to remove the permitted
development rights for the change of the use from a building and
any land within its curtilage from a use falling within Class C3
(dwellinghouse) of the Town and Country Planning (Use Classes)
(Amendment) (England) Order to a use falling within Class C4
(Houses in Multiple Occupation) of that Order being development
comprised within class L(b) of Part 3 of Schedule 2 to the Town and
Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) Order
2015 (as amended). The Article 4 direction is included at Appendix
One to the report.

 

To approve the required
notifications, as set out in the report and the publication of a
public notice as shown in Appendix One to the report.

 

Agree that officers undertake
consultation and notify the Secretary of State in accordance with
legislative requirements.

 

To approve that officers prepare a
further report, following the notification and consultation, of the
immediate Article 4 direction, to seek approval as to whether or
not to confirm this immediate Article 4 direction

 

6.     
Agree that officers undertake consultation and notify the Secretary
of State in accordance with legislative requirements.
 

7.     
To approve that officers prepare a further report, following the
notification and consultation, of the immediate Article 4
direction, to seek approval as to whether or not to confirm this
immediate Article 4 direction
 
Reasons for
decision:
 
An Article 4 Direction will
assist the Council in managing and regulating the growth of HMOs,
requiring planning permission for future conversions and improving
the ability to monitor and manage impacts on local
communities. It will improve the Council’s ability to
ensure the management standards of HMOs are maintained. An Article
4 direction is not an automatic ban on new HMOs. The Article 4
direction does not prevent the conversion of dwellings to HMOs, as
planning permission may still be granted for such conversions,
where they are appropriate, and can still provide a valuable role
in meeting housing needs.
 
Without the Direction, future
Local Plan policies on HMOs would have limited effect, as small HMO
conversions currently fall under permitted development
rights.
 
Other options
considered and rejected:
Option one: To introduce a
non-immediate Article 4 direction which does not take effect for a
set period of time after it is introduced (this period of time can
be any period from 28 days to 2 years, usually 12 months). The
non-immediate route was discounted because of the risk of a large
number of C3 to C4 conversions being carried out under permitted
development rights prior to the introduction of the measure, some
of which may not be granted planning permission where they are
required to apply for it.
 
Option Two: Do nothing – rejected as it
would leave the Council without control over HMO growth, increasing
risks of clustering, poor management, and negative impacts on
amenity.
topline: The Cabinet Member (Planning and Licensing) has decided to introduce a boroughwide Article 4 direction to regulate the growth of Houses in Multiple Occupation and require planning permission for future conversions.

decision_maker: Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member (Communities and Customers)
content:
Decision made:
 
1.   
To support the commissioning of a new
Asylum and Refugee Support and Signposting
Service in South Ribble.
 
2.   
To note that the Community Development team will
undertake a procurement process for South Ribble to identify a
suitable provider to deliver their own drop-in service.
 
3.   
For the cost of the service (£55,000) to be
met with the Asylum Dispersal Funding Grant.
 
Reasons for
decision:
 
The
previous Support and Signposting Service was commissioned by the
Lancashire County Council (LCC) Resettlement Team and delivered by
the British Red Cross. This contract concluded in October 2025, and
LCC has confirmed that it is no longer able to commission or fund a
replacement service. As a result, responsibility for ensuring
continuity of provision now rests with the District
Council.


Feedback from service users and partner organisations indicates
that the drop?in support model provides significant benefits to
refugees, asylum seekers and evacuees settling in South Ribble. The
South Ribble Community Integration Team has identified that the
absence of such a service would negatively impact the wellbeing,
independence and successful integration of resettled individuals.
Commissioning a new service will ensure that vulnerable residents
continue to have access to timely support, signposting and
community?based assistance.
 
Other options
considered and rejected:
 
A joint
commissioning approach with Chorley Council was explored. This
option was not progressed, as Chorley Council has an existing
preferred provider who is unable to deliver services within South
Ribble.
topline: The Deputy Leader and Cabinet Member (Communities and Customers) has decided to support the commissioning of a new Asylum and Refugee Support and Signposting Service in South Ribble.

To appoint George Cox & Sons Ltd on a NEC4
Engineering and Construction Contract, Option B (priced Main Works
with Bill of Quantities) form of contract to enable the delivery of
the Kingsfold & Middleforth package.
 
To note the Construction Procurement Strategy
was approved at Cabinet in March 2025, with all future contract
awards along with any amendments to this strategy are delegated to
the Executive Member. This appointment aligns with the approved
Construction Procurement Strategy for the Penwortham

To acknowledge in light

agreed scheme for Liverpool Road, this package will be tendered

award.

quality basis, that they offer value for money, have the necessary
skills and experience and that they will provide social
value. George Cox & Sons

tender that they are a competent contractor to deliver the
works.  This decision is necessary to comply with the
Council’s contract procedure rules and Constitution.
 
To allow the delivery of
the Kingsfold &
Middleforth developments.  
 
To ensure that the Penwortham Masterplan
delivery programme is progressed
 
Other options
considered and rejected:
 
To not progress with the Kingsfold &
Middleforth project. This has been rejected as this is a
Corporate Project and this wouldn’t align with the
pressing timescales. 
 
To retender the Principal Contractor for
Kingsfold & Middleforth. This has been rejected as the robust
competitive tender process
has demonstrated that George Cox & Sons Ltd
offer the most economically advantageous tender for this
tender.

content:
A Licensing Panel convened on Monday, 15
December 2025 consisting of three members, Councillor James Gleeson
(Chair), Councillor Chris Lomax and Councillor Lesley Pritchard, to
consider an application for a new premises licence for Fairway
Fusion, 20-22 Chapel Brow, Leyland.
 
The Applicant, Jack Thornton was present at
the hearing.
 
Also present at the hearing were the other
parties; Mr Peter Flynn and Tom Peil. 
 
The Licensing Manager outlined the report and
explained that members were asked to determine the application
submitted under Section 17 of the Licensing Act 2003, as six
relevant representations had been received from members of the
public.
 
Members were advised that, no representations
had been received from any of the responsible authorities.
 
The Licensing Manager explained that any
representations that relate to planning, highways or non-licensing
issues should not be taken into consideration when determining the
application.
 
The Applicants had applied for a licence on 23
October 2025 and sought the following:
 
Premises Opening
Hours
Sunday to Thursday    
               
05:00 - 24:00
Friday and
Saturday        
           05:00
- 02:00
 
Supply of
Alcohol
Sunday to Thursday    
              09:00
– 23:00
Friday and
Saturday        
         09:00 –
01:30

Live Music (Indoors)Friday and
Saturday    
              23:00
- 01:00

Sunday        
                                   
23:00 - 24:00

Recorded Music
(Indoors)
Sunday to Thursday    
            
23:00 - 24:00
Friday and
Saturday        
        23:00 - 02:00

Members noted that the Applicants had also supplied some
proposed
Conditions agreed with the Police, which were
enclosed in the supplementary agenda.
 
The Licensing Manager advised members of the
options available to them under Section 18 of the Licensing Act
2003 when determining the application.
In response to an enquiry from the Panel, the
Licensing Manager confirmed that the Police were happy with the
proposed conditions and for the application to be approved. It was
also confirmed that no noise complaints had been received by
Environmental Health for any premises in the vicinity, in the last
two years.
 

Applicant
 
The Applicant, addressed the Panel and gave an
overview of the premises layout, explaining that it would be an
indoor golf simulation venue, welcoming existing golf players and
new players. The venue would support local community and enable
golfers to play year-round, offering an alternative to traditional
golf courses.
 
The Applicant explained that the club house
would provide additional sports offerings such as darts and would
be a welcoming environment well suited for small events.
 
In order to comply with the four licensing
objectives, the applicant advised that the following would be
implemented:
 

An extensive CCTV camera system
would be fitted, covering both indoors and outdoors
A CCTV maintenance register would be
compiled and monitored at least once a month, alongside an incident
log and unauthorised sales log.
Staff would be trained on Challenge
25 and given refresher training every 12 months and the venue would
be a member of Pub Watch.
The premises would be compliant with
fire safety regulations and a fire risk assessment in place before
opening.
Staff would be first aid
trained.
Door Supervisors would be in place
as agreed with the Police and an online booking system would be
used to anticipate how busy the premises will be.
There are no plans for any external
speakers to be fitted.
Challenge 25 would be in place at
the venue alongside a refusal register, under 18s would not be
permitted in the venue after 9pm unless it is for a small private
function, of which they will need to leave before 1am.

 

Questions to the Applicant

 
In response to the Panel, the Applicants
confirmed they would be willing to fit a noise monitoring
system.

The other parties referred to the opening
times of the premises and the times requested for serving alcohol
and asked if it would change from being a golf venue to a bar
during the weekend. The Applicant confirmed that the purpose of the
venue was a golf simulator and the bar was for those patrons.
 
The Applicant explained that the opening times
were extended in order to accommodate for shift workers, widening
the potential clientele.
 
The Other parties asked what reasonable steps
would be taken to manage noise and public nuisance. The Applicant
explained that they didn’t anticipate much noise leakage as
the simulators were insulated with sound absorbent padding and
insulated between the panels. The Club House would not have loud
music every day as it would be more of a casual venue.
 
The Applicant confirmed that noise leakage
would come from egress and ingress, but the property had no windows
that could open.
 
The Other Parties asked how the Applicants
intended to communicate with local residents. In response, the
Applicant confirmed that they had spoken to one of the objectors
frequently when he visited the premises. Following being notified
of the outcome of the hearing, it was their intention to send
unaddressed letters to local residents providing contact details
for the applicants.
 

Other Parties
  
The Other Parties addressed the Panel.
 
Mr Flynn advised that there were currently
four licensed establishments on Chapel Brow all open until early
hours of the morning, when patrons exit the bars intoxicated.
 
The location of Fairway is in close proximity
to residential areas. It was his view that the proposed operating
hours and playing of music would pose risk of disturbance to
residents living nearby.
 
Mr Flynn also raised concerns about patrons
congregating and smoking outside of the premises and noted there
was no provision for a dedicated smoking area. Mr Flynn stated that
it would be impossible to enforce a dispersal policy once customers
had left the premises.
 
Mr Flynn asked that Members consider adding a
condition to require two mandatory door supervisors at the premises
Friday and Saturday starting at 8pm.
 
Mr Peel addressed the Panel and explained that
his home was directly opposite the premises, and it was less than
50ft from his bedroom window. He explained that the premises
playing live music until 2am would cause significant disruption to
his ability to sleep and enjoy his home environment. Mr Flynn also
made reference to Article 8 of the European Convention on Human
Rights.
 
Mr Peel stated that the premises should have a
curfew of midnight, with no outdoor speakers permitted and no open
windows or doors.
 
The Applicant’s responded to the
concerns raised by the other parties and explained that they were
not seeking to make a profit and had heavily invested into the
venue to ensure it was accessible for everyone.
 
The Police had suggested the timings for the
door supervisors, and it would be their role to assist with any
disorder at the premises and to encourage patrons to leave quietly.
The Applicant also explained that there would be a smoking area at
the side of the premises, monitored with CCTV.
 
The Applicant asked Mr Peel if he had heard
any noise over the last two weeks from the renovation work. In
response, Mr Peel advised that he did not hear any noise from
Fairways but could hear noise pollution from Rimmers Music, which
normally concludes by 8:30-9pm.
 
The Applicant reassured the Other Parties
there wouldn’t be noise leakage from the venue and explained
that they would direct music speakers towards the rear of the
property.
 
The Panel sought clarification on some of the
representations heard from other parties and if these would be
admissible to a Licensing Hearing.
 
The Licensing Manager confirmed that any
representation made in relation to the building, parking and
highways are planning matters and not relevant to the licensing
objectives and should not be considered as part of the
hearing. 

 

Sum Up
 
The Other Parties addressed the Panel and
referred to the impact that the premises would have on local
residents in relation to noise and dispersal at the premises. They
requested that a sound limiter be added to the premises which would
help in reducing noise.
 
The Applicant explained that they were
veterans trying to create a community and that door supervisors
would monitor the sound levels outside as well as any congregating
patrons. The bar staff would determine when to stop serving
individuals if they believed them to be intoxicated. The Applicant
explained that the venue was primarily a golf led venue with some
hospitality to complement that aspect of the business. They were
committed to conforming with licensing objectives and did not want
to detract from community wellbeing. 
 
Resolved:
 
In reaching its decision
the Panel considered the following:
 

Both Written and Oral Evidence
presented in connection with the hearing
The Guidance issued under Section
182 of the Licensing Act 2003
The Council’s Statement of
Licensing Policy effective from 2025
The Licensing Act 2003

 
The Panel carefully considered all the
evidence provided by the parties at the hearing together with the
written representations.
 
The Panel determined to grant the application
as applied for.
 
The Panel considered Section 7.2 of the
statutory S182 Guidance. Panel members gave appropriate weight to
the fact that no responsible authorities had objected to the
application and conditions had been agreed to mitigate any
concerns, responsible authorities under the Licensing Act 2003 are
expected to be experts within their field.
 
The Panel were of the view that although the
additional volunteered conditions would help to address the issues
raised within the representations, members requested that the
additional conditions would be imposed upon the licence to promote
the licensing objectives. 
 
The Panel have decided to impose the following
conditions to the premises Licence:
 

The DPS or other
responsible member of staff will conduct due diligence checks of
noise emanating from the premises at the nearest noise sensitive
residential location after 21:00 hours every 30 minutes that
regulated entertainment is taking place at the
premises. 

 

A written record
shall be maintained of the checks undertaken and shall include the
date, time and result of the checks, the name of the person making
the record and a note of any remedial action taken should noise
levels be deemed too loud.

 

Were complaints are
made from local residents regarding noise emanating from the
premises, steps will be taken to reduce the levels sufficiently to
mitigate further complaints.   

 

A sound limiting
device shall be fitted to the sound system. 

 
a)     
All entertainment shall be played through this device.
 
b)    
The device shall be set in accordance with the Environmental Health
Department to a level where it is unlikely to cause a public
nuisance to residents in the immediate vicinity of the
premises.
 
c)     
After 23:00 hours all doors/windows to the premises shall remain
closed during opening hours save for access and egress.
 
d)    
No waste including glass to be deposited in outside waste
receptacles between the hours of 19:00 and 12:00.
 

The premises shall
operate and maintain a CCTV system which shall be used during all
times licensable activities are taking place at the premises and
comply as follows:-

 
a)           
The system shall cover all entrances and exits of the premises,
including the smoking shelter, in addition to covering areas of the
premises used to store alcohol.
b)        The focus of
the camera(s) shall be so as to enable clear identification of
persons on the premises.
c)        The system
will be capable of time and date stamping recordings and
retaining the said recordings
for at least 21 days.
d)        The Data
Controller shall make footage available to a Police
Officer
or Licensing Officer,
where such a request is made in accordance with the principles of
the Data Protection Act or any subsequent or alternative
legislation.
e)        Signage
advising that CCTV is in operation.
 

A written dispersal
policy shall be formulated and adhered to.

 

A risk assessment
will be conducted by the DPS outlining the necessity for door
supervisors to be used at the premises. 

 

A drugs policy will
be drawn up and always implemented at the premises the premises is
open to the public.

 

The drugs policy will
detail what actions are expected of staff and door supervisors
should illegal drugs be found or customers be suspected of either
possessing or having taken illegal drugs. A copy of the drugs
policy will be made available to the police and licensing authority
on request.

 

An incident register
will be maintained at the premises, and any details of public order
offences will be recorded. Said register will be made available
upon request to an authorised officer.

 
The Panel felt that after careful
consideration of the case before them, an appropriate and
proportionate decision had been reached. 
 
All parties to the hearing, have the right to
appeal the decision to the Magistrates Court within 21 days.

content:
A Licensing Panel convened on Monday, 17
November 2025 consisting of three members, Councillor James Gleeson
(Chair), Councillor Chris Lomax and Councillor Lesley Pritchard, to
consider an application for a review of the premises licence for
The Ship, 165 Towngate, Leyland, PR25 2TE.
 
The Applicant for review, Mr Matthew Cropper
and the Premises Licence Holder Mr Dean Walsh were present at the
hearing.
 
The Licensing Officer outlined the report and
advised that a responsible authority may ask the licensing
authority to review a premises licence, at any stage following the
initial grant of the licence.
 
Environmental Health as Responsible Authority
had made an application for the review of The Ship on the grounds
that the premises were undermining the licensing objective of
Public Nuisance.
 
Members noted that the application for review
was included as a background document and two further supplementary
packs had been provided by Environmental Health. Four
representations had been received from other parties and had been
included as Appendix B. The Licensing Officer advised that the
other parties were unable to attend the hearing so he would present
their representations.
 
Under Section 51 of the Licensing Act 2003 the
Licensing Authority placed notices at the premises as per the
regulations, which were subsequently placed out of view in the
premises, displayed in an upstairs window by the Premises Licence
Holder.
 
When determining the application for review,
members noted the options available to them.
 
Questions to the
Licensing Officer
 
Members sought clarification on the
circumstances surrounding the first set of notices. The Licensing
Officer explained that the Premises Licence Holder moved the
notices to an upstairs window, where they would not be visible to
members of the public. Officers were made aware of this and had
evidence of the correct positioning of the notices when they were
initially placed.
 
The Premises Licence Holder asked how many
notices should be visible at the premises and the Licensing Officer
explained that two were placed on the lamppost outside of the
property.
 
The Premises Licence Holder raised concerns
around the delivery and placement of the notices and Officer
behaviour. The Licence Holder also referred to the notices
appearing on the Licensing Authorities website late.
 
The Panel’s Legal Advisor addressed the
Premises Licence Holder and advised that they had not been
prejudiced as the notice was required to let the public know of the
review. As the premises had been served with a notice, which was
displayed this was enough to notify the public.
 
The Premises Licence Holder stated that there
should only be one notice made visible at the property, and he was
advised to take the extra notices down.
 
Applicant for
Review
 
Mr Cropper, on behalf of Environmental Health,
addressed the Panel and explained that the purpose of the review
was to protect residents from public nuisance and that his service
had been dealing with noise complaints since November 2024.
 
Mr Cropper admitted that these complaints did
begin before the current Premises Licence Holder took over the
premises.
 
Members noted that the premises was close to
residential properties and originally began as a restaurant that
had gradually changed into a bar. There had been a planning
application and noise assessment, however some of the conditions
had not been implemented.
 
Mr Cropper explained that he was hoping to
solve the noise issues raised by residents, in particular the bass
noise which could be heard inside residential properties. It was
his view that the issues could be addressed by way of
conditions.
 
All parties to the hearing were played
recordings of the noise from The Ship, which had been taken from
the living room of a nearby residential property at midnight on 31
August 2025.
 
Mr Cropper confirmed that he had been out to
visit the premises and could hear the noise clearly and identify
its origin.
 
Questions to the
Applicant
 
The Applicant confirmed that complaints had
been received about the gables and these had been resolved, the
complainant had advised that they hadn’t heard noise from the
gables.
 
The recordings were all taken from the living
room of a nearby residential property, Mr Cropper confirmed that he
had also stood on the front doorstep, walked past the premises and
could confirm it was coming from The Ship.
 
In response to a question from the
Panel’s Legal Advisor, Mr Cropper explained that the sound
machine would be set up at the complainant’s property on a
Friday and left for a number of days,
the complainant would press the machine when they could hear a
noise,
 
Mr Cropper confirmed that when he visited the
complainant and walked past the premises, the internal and external
doors were closed at the time.
 
The Panel’s Legal Advisor referred to
the proposed conditions provided from Environmental Health and
asked if they would consider setting a decibel level on the
conditions. In response, Mr Cropper explained that decibel limits
should be set above background level noise, as the road is quite
loud during the day and quiet at night, he would want to take
advice from colleagues or refer to British Standards surrounding
noise abatement.
 
In response to a question, Mr Cropper
confirmed that the significant amount of diary evidence provided by
one of the complainants established the pattern of noise to be
weekends and evenings, becoming a nuisance when traffic
reduces.
 
The Panel’s Legal Advisor sought
clarification that the Applicant for Review was still happy with
the proposed conditions. In response, Mr Cropper confirmed that he
was.
 
The Premises Licence Holder explained that he
did not want residents to experience distress, they believed the
complainant to be one lady who they had since spoken to and
resolved her issues. The Licence Holder advised that since meeting
with Environmental Health the premises management had begun taking
decibel readings and a new door had been fitted.
 
The Premises Licence Holder invited officers
to visit the premises on a Saturday.
 
The Premises Licence Holder advised that since
he took over the bar he had been targeted by the Police and Fire
Service and felt attacked when he was trying to run a business. He
admitted that he did lose his temper with officers as he felt
persecuted, having received visits from the Council, Fire Brigade,
Police and Environmental Health all in one week.
 
The Premises Licence Holder asked if the
complaint was purely noise based, and Mr Cropper confirmed that it
was.
 
The Premises Licence Holder stated that he
would have preferred Mr Cropper to play a recording of the noise
that he had obtained himself, not from the complainant.
 
Other Parties
 
On behalf of the Other Parties the Licensing
Officer read out their representations and highlighted the
following concerns:

·         There
should be a noise limiter according to planning conditions.

·         The front
door is closed but internal lobby door open allowing noise to
escape.

·         The
outdoor seating area should be vacated by 21:00pm but has patrons
outside until midnight.

·         Ongoing
noise issues with excessive noise late at night with loud music

·         Patrons
leaving the pub showing disruptive behaviour and
shouting/swearing.

·         Can only
sleep around 1:30am during the weekend.
 
Premises Licence
Holder
 
The Premises Licence Holder addressed the
Panel and explained that he thought it would only be Fridays and
Saturdays causing an issue as he had been closing at 23:30pm every
other night because they had no business. There had only been one
police attendance since he had the licence for the premises and no
fighting.
 
The Licence Holder stated that he had spoken
to nearby residents and had invested a lot of money into making The
Ship a proper business.
 
Members asked if the Premises Licence Holder
would be willing to fit a noise limiter and supply data
periodically to the Environmental Health Officers. The Premises
Licence Holder confirmed that he would.
 
The Premises Licence Holder also confirmed
that the premises keeps a diary of decibel recordings.
 
The Panel’s Legal Advisor asked Mr Walsh
if he had more representations to add and emphasised that the
Council wanted to work with the premises. The Legal Representative
referred to incidents which had occurred with officers and
reassured the Premises Licence Holder that they were only doing
their job and sought clarification that the incidents would not
happen again.
 
The Premises Licence Holder explained that he
felt intimidated and accepted that he made comments that he
shouldn’t have and apologised.
 
The Panel’s Legal Advisor clarified that
the hearing was fair and procedurally correct.
 
Sum Up
 
Mr Cropper advised that he was confident the
noise issues could be solved with technology and careful management
by way of additional conditions. The application could have been
resolved by way of a minor variation had the PLH received better
advice. In order for Environmental
Health to have these conditions added they have had to apply for a
review.
 
The Premises Licence Holder advised that his
representative advised him to have the hearing deferred until
January.
 
Resolved:
 
In reaching its decision
the Panel considered the following:
 

Both Written and Oral Evidence
presented in connection with the hearing
The Guidance issued under Section
182 of the Licensing Act 2003
The Council’s Statement of
Licensing Policy effective from 2020
The Licensing Act 2003


The Panel carefully considered all the
evidence provided by the parties at the hearing together with the
written representations.
 
The Panel considered that noise from the
premises did impact on neighbouring residents and that additional
control measures were necessary and proportionate to promote the
prevention of public nuisance. To uphold the licensing objective of
prevention of public nuisance, the following conditions now apply
to the premises licence:
 
1.The premises licence holder shall install
and maintain an Automatic Volume Control System (AVCS) for all
amplified live or recorded music indoors and must be installed
within one month of the date of this decision. The agreed noise
limit will also be agreed with Environmental Health within one
month of the date of this decision or when the AVCS is installed
whichever is sooner. The system shall comply as follows:
 
a)     
the AVCS shall be calibrated and set so that the amplified sound
level at the boundary of the premises does not exceed the agreed
noise limit with Environmental Health (EH). The approved limiter
shall be set to ensure that the resulting sound cannot be heard at
neighbouring properties.
 
b)    
The AVCS shall automatically adjust the volume to maintain
compliance and shall not be manually overridden. The approved
limiter shall be set to ensure that the resulting sound cannot be
heard at neighbouring properties.
 
b) The AVCS shall be installed by a competent
technician and shall be tested and certified by a competent
engineer. A copy of the commissioning/installation report shall be
supplied to the Licensing Authority and retained on the
premises.
 
c) The AVCS shall be in operation at any time
the premises is authorised to carry on licensable activity and
shall operate automatically, without intervention to maintain the
required limit. Any temporary disablement or failure must be
reported to the designated premises supervisor and the Licensing
Authority within 24 hours; a failure shall be rectified as a matter
of urgency.
 
d) The AVCS shall be maintained in good
working order, with servicing and calibration at least every 12
months by a competent technician. A records log shall be kept on
the premises, recording dates of service, calibration values, and
any adjustments, and shall be made available for inspection by the
Licensing Authority and EH on request.
 
e) The designated premises supervisor shall be
responsible for ensuring the AVCS remains functional during
licensed hours and for notifying the Licensing Authority of any
faults or failures.
 
f) On receipt of any complaints made to the
Local Authority, Licensing Team or Environmental Health then the
sound limiter shall be set in conjunction with the Environmental
Section of the Council.
 
g) The DPS or other responsible member of
staff will conduct due diligence checks of noise emanating from the
premises at the nearest noise sensitive residential location after
21:00 hours every 30 minutes that regulated entertainment is taking
place at the premises.  A written record
shall be maintained of the checks undertaken and shall include the
date, time and result of the checks, the name of the person making
the record and a note of any remedial action taken should noise
levels be deemed too loud.
 
h) Where complaints are made from local residents regarding noise emanating from the
premises, steps will be taken to reduce the levels sufficiently to
mitigate further complaints
 
Whilst it was discussed at the hearing that
conditions should be imposed only on the weekend, Members felt that
the above conditions should be in place Monday – Sunday as
suggested by the original report by Environmental Health.
 
Warning
 
Mr Walsh is formally advised that as the
Premises Licence Holder you are required to act professionally,
cooperate with authorised officers and ensure that the premises is
managed responsibly at all times. This
includes:
 
·        
Engaging respectfully and appropriately with Licensing,
Environmental Health, Police and other responsible authorities;
·        
Providing accurate information when requested;
·        
Demonstrating responsible management and decision-making
 
Failure to meet these responsibilities may
result in further action including:
 

Licence Review
Additional Conditions being
considered
Potential enforcement action

 
 
Members wanted to ensure that Mr Walsh knows
that:
 

1.     
His conduct toward officers and responsible authorities is
appropriate, professional and cooperative at
all times.
 

2.     
Any future interactions do not repeat the behaviour exhibited
previously such as taking down Legal notices at the premises,
swearing or shouting at officers.
 

3.     
He take immediate steps to review his
approach to officers going forward.
 
Continued concerns may lead the Licensing
Authority to consider more actions.
 
This warning will be placed on your licensing
record and may be considered in any future proceedings or
enforcement.
 
All parties to the hearing, have the right to
appeal the decision to the Magistrates Court within 21 days.

content:
A Licensing Panel convened on Wednesday, 5
November 2025 consisting of three members, Councillor James Gleeson
(Chair), Councillor Chris Lomax and Councillor Hilary Bedford, to
consider an application for a new premises licence for 1896 Lounge,
55 Hough Lane, Leyland.
 
The Applicants, Kathryn Lonsdale and Josh
Lonsdale were present at the hearing.
 
Also present at the hearing were the other
parties;
 
The Licensing Manager outlined the report and
explained that members were asked to determine the application in
line with the Licensing Act 2003, as two relevant representations
had been received from members of the public. One of which, was a
petition. Members noted that petitions were accepted under the
Licensing Act 2003 but only the “instigator” of the
petition would be invited to speak at the hearing and provided with
a copy of the officer’s report.
 
No representations had been received from any
of the responsible authorities.
 
The Licensing Manager explained the
representations were only relevant if they could demonstrate an
undermining of at least one of the four licensing objectives and
they were not frivolous or vexatious.
 
The Applicants had applied for a licence on 19
September 2025 and sought the following:
 
Live Music (Indoors)Sunday
– Thursday    
               
11:00-23:30
Friday –
Saturday        
               
11:00-00:30

Christmas Eve, New Years    11:00-02:00
Eve and Bank Holidays

Recorded Music (Indoors)
Sunday –
Thursday    
               
11:00-23:30
Friday –
Saturday        
               
11:00-00:30

Christmas Eve, New Years    11:00-02:00
Eve and Bank Holidays
 
Supply of Alcohol
(on and off)
Sunday –
Thursday    
               
11:00-23:00
Friday –
Saturday        
               
11:00-00:30

Christmas Eve, New Years    11:00-02:00
Eve and Bank Holidays
 
Premises Opening
Hours
Sunday –
Thursday    
               
11:00-00:30
Friday –
Saturday        
               
11:00-01:30

Christmas Eve, New Years    11:00-02:00
Eve and Bank Holidays

Members noted that the Applicants had also supplied some
proposed
conditions, which were enclosed in the
supplementary agenda.
 

Applicant
 
The Applicant, Josh Lonsdale addressed the
Panel and explained that they had submitted their statement in
advance to demonstrate that they were willing to work with the
local community.
 
Assurances were given that the premises would
not be operated in the same manner as former businesses at the
premises had. The previous establishment had a business model based
on high volume sales and loud music, whereas Lounge 1896 would be a
premium small capacity cocktail bar aimed at mature clientele.
 
The Applicant explained that live music would
only be acoustic as the venue was not a night club, there would be
no late-night promotions and the
premises would seek to promote the crime and disorder licensing
objective.
 
A refusal log would be kept on site, staff
would be trained in conflict management, and the premises would
operate schemes such as Challenge 25 and Ask Angela. There would be
a zero-tolerance policy on drugs and weapons, with toilet areas
being checked every thirty minutes. The premises would also be
joining Pubwatch.
 
The Applicant advised that there had been no
objections from responsible authorities and there would be a
limited delivery window of 9-5, they accepted there was limited
parking on Hough Lane and explained they had a different plan for
deliveries if needed.
 
In relation to the Public Nuisance objective,
the Applicant explained that there would be a full noise management
plan, doors and windows would be kept closed. There would also be
no external speakers or amplified music. The Applicant also advised
they would put a noise cancelling device in the premises.
 
The Applicant stated that live performances
would hopefully end by 11pm Sunday-Thursday and midnight
Friday-Saturday, but the premises would like extra hours over the
Christmas Period. There would be a customer dispersal policy and
outdoor smoking area. No drinks would be permitted outside
after 10pm and the outdoor seating area would also close by
10pm during the week. Under 18s would not be allowed into the
premises after 8pm unless attending a private or family
function.
 
The Applicant emphasised they wanted to work
on community engagement and with residents, contact details of
management for the premises would be provided and there would be
monthly meetings.
 

Questions to the Applicant

 
The Panel sought clarification and further
detail on the proposed noise action plan. In response, the
Applicant stated there would be music and sound controls in place,
to be managed by the Designated Premises Supervisor (DPS) and Duty
Manager throughout the evenings. There would also be outdoor area
controls, and noise controls put in place to manage deliveries and
waste disposal.
 
The Other Parties referred to the previous
premises and asked how 1896 would differ in terms of noise
pollution. In response, the Applicant advised that he could share
their draft noise management action plan but the speaker system
which was fitted in Bar 55 was being completely taken out and a
smaller system put in place. The fixed seating had also been
removed so live music acts could be moved around the venue, they
wouldn’t be performing in front of the glass
windows. 
 
The Licensing Manager suggested that a
condition could be imposed in conjunction with Environmental
Health, requiring that the premises has a noise management plan and
agreed noise level established by a qualified person before
opening.
 

Other Parties
 
The Licensing Manager introduced a
representation on behalf of an objector who couldn’t attend.
The representation made reference to
noise disturbance, parking issues, noise from car doors opening and
closing and noise levels from the premises customers.
 
The Other Parties addressed the Panel and
referred to parking issues, explaining that it was difficult to
park on Hough Lane and customers would not use the local car
parks.
 
There were no questions to the other
parties.
 
In light of the
representations heard the Chair asked the Applicant if they wished
to make any amendments to their application. The Applicant
confirmed that they were happy with the application as is.
 

 

Sum Up
 
The Other Parties addressed the Panel and
advised that there are elderly residents who live on Newsome Street
and music playing until 2AM would disturb children sleeping,
especially on Christmas Eve.
 
The Applicant advised that he wanted to work
with residents and committed to installing a noise canceller. He
also assured residents that the only late opening would be New
Years Eve and that Leyland would benefit from the bar opening. The
Applicant also explained they wanted to work with other bars in the
area to manage the flow of customers down the high street.
 
 
Resolved:
 
In reaching its decision
the Panel considered the following:
 

Both Written and Oral Evidence
presented in connection with the hearing
The Guidance issued under Section
182 of the Licensing Act 2003
The Council’s Statement of
Licensing Policy effective from 2020
The Licensing Act 2003

The Panel carefully considered all the
evidence provided by the parties at the hearing together with the
written representations.
 
The Panel determined to grant the application
as applied for including the timings and conditions volunteered
within the operating schedule and supplementary document provided
by the applicant.
 
The Panel considered Section 7.2 of the
statutory S182 Guidance. Panel members gave appropriate weight to
the fact that no responsible authorities, who are expected to be
experts within their field had objected to the application.
 
The Panel were of the view that although the
additional volunteered conditions would help to address the issues
raised within the representations, members requested that the
additional conditions would be imposed upon the licence to promote
the licensing objectives. 
 
The Panel have decided to impose the following
conditions to the premises Licence:
 

The DPS or other responsible member
of staff will conduct due diligence checks of noise emanating from
the premises at the nearest noise sensitive residential location
after 21:00 hours every 30 minutes that regulated entertainment is
taking place at the premises. 

 

A written record shall be maintained
of the checks undertaken and shall include the date, time and
result of the checks, the name of the person making the record and
a note of any remedial action taken should noise levels be deemed
too loud.

 

Were complaints are made from
local residents regarding noise
emanating from the premises, steps will be taken to reduce the
levels sufficiently to mitigate further complaints. 
 

 

A sound limiting device shall be
fitted to the sound system. 

 
a)     
All entertainment shall be played through this device.
 
b)    
The device shall be set in accordance with the Environmental Health
Department to a level where it is unlikely to cause a public
nuisance to residents in the immediate vicinity of the
premises.
 
c)     
After 23:00 hours all doors/windows to the premises shall remain
closed during opening hours save for access and egress.
 
d)    
No waste including glass to be deposited in outside waste
receptacles between the hours of 19:00 and 12:00.
 

The premises shall operate and
maintain a CCTV system which shall be used during all times
licensable activities are taking place at the premises and comply
as follows:-

 
a)           
The system shall cover all entrances and exits of the premises,
including the smoking shelter, in addition to covering areas of the
premises used to store alcohol.

b)        The focus of the
camera(s) shall be so as to enable clear
identification of persons on the premises.

c)        The system will
be capable of time and date stamping recordings and
retaining the said recordings for at least 21
days.

d)        The Data
Controller shall make footage available to a Police Officer
or Licensing Officer, where such a
request is made in accordance with the principles of the Data
Protection Act or any subsequent or alternative legislation.

e)        Signage advising
that CCTV is in operation.
 

A written dispersal policy shall be
formulated and adhered to.

 

A risk assessment will be conducted
by the DPS outlining the necessity for door supervisors to be used
at the premises. 

 

A drugs policy will be drawn up and
always implemented at the premises the premises is open to the
public.

 

The drugs policy will detail what
actions are expected of staff and door supervisors should illegal
drugs be found or customers be suspected of either possessing or
having taken illegal drugs. A copy of the drugs policy will be made
available to the police and licensing authority on request.

 

An incident register will be
maintained at the premises, and any details of public order
offences will be recorded. Said register will be made available
upon request to an authorised officer.

 
The Panel felt that after careful
consideration of the case before them, an appropriate and
proportionate decision had been reached. 
 
All parties to the hearing, have the right to
appeal the decision to the Magistrates Court within 21 days.
topline: The Licensing Panel has decided to grant a new premises licence for 1896 Lounge in Leyland, despite concerns raised by local residents about noise disturbance and parking issues.
